stories.title: ‘Arnab’ packs rain, not cyclone strength: Kolkata remains under weather alert
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: ‘Cyclone Arnab’ is officially a deep depression, but heavy rain, thunderstorms and gusty winds continue to threaten Bengal.
The word ‘cyclone’ may have been dominating social media feeds, but the India Meteorological Department has drawn a clear line: the system being referred to as ‘Arnab’ is not a cyclone.
It is a deep depression, and Kolkata still has plenty of rain to contend with.
The weather system over the Bay of Bengal has brought heavy rain, thunderstorms and gusty winds across parts of Bengal, Odisha and Andhra Pradesh.
But despite the growing public attention around it, the system has not attained the wind speed required for classification as a cyclonic storm.
The deep depression currently has maximum sustained winds of 55-65 kmph, with gusts reaching 75 kmph.
Under the IMD's classification, a deep depression has an average wind speed of 50-61 kmph, while a cyclonic storm requires wind speeds of 62-88 kmph.
That distinction matters because the system widely being described online as “Cyclone Arnab” does not officially qualify for the cyclone tag.
According to the IMD, the deep depression over the north Andhra Pradesh coast moved slowly west-northwestwards at around 3 kmph at 6 am.
It crossed the coast close to southwest of Kalingapatnam between 11 pm on September 23 and 1 am on September 24, carrying maximum sustained winds of 55-65 kmph and gusts of up to 75 kmph.
The system subsequently moved west-northwestwards and was located over north coastal Andhra Pradesh.
It was around 50 km west of Kalingapatnam, 80 km north-northeast of Visakhapatnam and 170 km southwest of Gopalpur in Odisha.

article_sentences: The High Court of Karnataka on Thursday ordered issue of notice to the Election Commission of India (ECI) and MLA for Srirangapatna.

A.B. Ramesha Bandisidde Gowda, on a petition which has questioned a special court rejecting criminal prosecution of the MLA for allegedly not disclosing certain immovable properties in his affidavit for the 2023 Assembly elections.

It has been claimed in the petition that the petitioner had initially issued notice to the MLA, who admitted ownership but cited contractual arrangements through general power of attorney and liabilities in favour of a third party, as a reason for non-disclosure in the affidavit.

Contending that the MLA was the owner of the properties despite contractual agreement, the petitioner had lodged a complaint with the Chief Electoral Officer (CEO), Karnataka, for initiation of action against the MLA.
When no response was received, the petitioner had filed a private complaint with the special court.
Further hearing was adjourned till October 15.

article_sentences: A pro-Left Syndicate member in the University of Calicut has claimed that the proposal to revamp the rules related to college union election was approved at a recent meeting without detailed discussions.

K. Mohamed Haneefa, the Syndicate member, said in a statement on Thursday (September 24, 2026) that the report of a panel that studied the proposed reforms to the election rules was presented as an “out-of-agenda” item without being circulated to members in advance.
The report was objected to by some members who sought adequate time for examination and discussion, he said.
Mr. Haneefa also criticised the move to form a Calicut University Research Scholars’ Union for all full-time PhD research scholars.

He said that more clarity was required on how their academic and social links with the student community of the host institution would be maintained while they were being brought under a separate university-level union.

The geographical distribution of research scholars across the university campus and affiliated colleges also should be considered while designing a representative structure that can ensure effective participation and communication, he added.

article_sentences: Issues with Form 6, filled out by first-time voters, were among the 14 objections recorded by the two Election Commissioners over various ECI decisions in the past 10 months.
The poll panel has now issued a clarification on it.

The Election Commission said there has been "no change" to the existing Form 6, after an investigation by the Indian Express found that two Election Commissioners formally objected to alterations in the document that is required to be filled out to register as a new voter.
The poll panel pointed out that the new section on SIR had been added as a separate annexure, without any modification to the original Form 6 itself.
The issue was among the 14 objections recorded by Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi over various ECI decisions in the past 10 months.
WHAT IS THE ROW OVER FORM 6?
One key objection concerned a new section added to Form 6, which is required to be filled by first-time voters.
The existing Form 6 asks for basic personal details, like proof of age and proof of address.
From July, it required new voters to state whether they, their parents, or grandparents had been listed on the electoral roll after the last SIR.
Crucially, new applicants could not proceed or submit the form without answering it.
In several states, the last SIR was held in the early 2000s.
The SIR declaration was added directly to the online form, rather than through a formal amendment to the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960.

stories.title: Election Commission rift reaches Supreme Court: Advocate seeks contempt action against Gyanesh Kumar

article_sentences: A Supreme Court advocate has sought the Attorney General’s consent to initiate criminal contempt proceedings against CEC Gyanesh Kumar over alleged violations of the Election Commission’s multi-member functioning.

New Delhi: As many as 14 written objections in 10 months, allegations of key electoral decisions being taken without the knowledge of two Election Commissioners, and now a bid to initiate criminal contempt proceedings against Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar.

The internal differences within the Election Commission of India (ECI) have taken a legal turn, with a Supreme Court advocate seeking the Attorney General of India’s consent to move the apex court against the CEC.
Advocate Brajesh Singh on Thursday, September 24, sought statutory consent from Attorney General R Venkataramani to initiate criminal contempt proceedings against Kumar.
His request comes in the wake of a report in The Indian Express that highlighted what it described as a breakdown of consensus within the three-member Election Commission.
Singh has cited the report alleging that Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi formally recorded their objections at least 14 times over the past 10 months.
According to the report, the objections related to several decisions concerning the functioning of the poll panel and the management of electoral rolls.
Among the issues cited by Singh are changes to voter-registration software, alterations to Form 6 and the deletion and restoration of voter names during the Special Intensive Revision process.

The advocate alleged that the two Election Commissioners had described several such actions as 'unauthorised' and 'illegal', claiming they were undertaken without their knowledge or the approval of the full Commission.

Singh has argued that the alleged conduct amounts to a violation of the institutional framework governing the Election Commission and runs contrary to Supreme Court judgments dealing with the functioning of the poll panel.
He specifically referred to the Supreme Court's judgments in TN Seshan versus Union of India and Anoop Baranwal versus Union of India.
According to Singh, these judgments establish the importance of the Election Commission functioning as a multi-member constitutional body.

stories.headline: How Ather’s foray into mass market pits it against giant incumbents TVS, Bajaj
stories.title: How Ather’s foray into mass market pits it against giant incumbents TVS, Bajaj
stories.summary: Dressed in a black tee and blue jeans, Tarun Mehta walked across the stage in a hall packed with nearly 5,000 people. The co-founder and CEO of Ather Energy had run through the sequence the day before—where to pause, where to slow down and where to let a joke land. It also had him pretending to be a regular office commuter with a laptop bag and a lunchbox in his hands who opens the luggage space of his scooter with a tap of the knee.But dry runs do not prepare you fully for a roomful of enthusiasts. Every time a new feature of the Konarc, Ather’s newest scooter, flashed on the giant screen behind Mehta, the hall erupted in cheers, screams and whistles, occasionally leaving him wondering what it was that clicked.The big picture of Ather’s journey since it started in 2013 holds no such riddles for Mehta. Others might question, as they did back then, why he and his co-founder Swapnil Jain were not doing ecommerce [every other Indian startup was] and, instead, choosing deeptech hardware.Those doubts would be silenced by the cheers arising from that hall in Bengaluru on August 29. It was Ather Community Day, an annual gathering the Bengaluru-based company has held since 2016 when it had no product. A grand total of 30 people attended it that year. Ten years and three products later, the event pulled in 5,000.The cheers Mehta relishes more will be outside that hall, in the rough and tumble of the two-wheeler market. Konarc is Ather’s first e-scooter to be priced below ₹1 lakh, a whole ₹1 below the psychological threshold. So far, its cheapest was the Rizta, whose pricing started at ₹121,999. Both prices are without its software pack, which ranges between ₹8,500 and ₹23,500.The Konarc takes Ather headlong into a rivalry with TVS and Bajaj, two of the four—Hero MotoCorp and Honda Motorcycle and Scooter India (HMSI) are the other two—that have dominated India’s two-wheeler market for decades and flexed their distribution muscle and strong balance sheets to rise to the top in electric two-wheelers. The mass market is where consumers come less for tech and features and more for the everyday reliability that the legacy guys have proven to be good at.About half the e-scooter market is in the ₹1-1.25 lakh price range. With the new scooter, Ather has a product for 90 percent of the market, claims Mehta.That also means this segment has 100 percent attention from everyone.While this battle plays out as a challenger takes on incumbents in a new playground, its outcome will signal whether a new era of two-wheeler leadership in India is on the anvil. Not only did Ather tear up the Indian startup rule book by going into deeptech hardware, it also refused to follow the rules of the two-wheeler industry.India’s automotive history, two- and four-wheelers alike, was built by companies that thrived in partnerships with multinationals in their early years. Ather is doing it on its own, obsessing over product in an industry focussed on functionality instead of making the best products in the world.The focus on functionality is best embodied by the seven decades of scooters in India. It has always been the thing that takes you from point A to B. It did not need to have a touchscreen dashboard or alerts about the next pothole. It did not need to tell you cricket match scores or send an SOS to your emergency contacts. Yet, these are the things you get when you buy an Ather and opt for its paid software platform, AtherStack Pro. It is not just the whim of a couple of tech bros. Nine out of 10 Ather buyers opt for the software bundle. “You have to bring out features that make sense at a cost that makes sense [and the customer will pay for it],” says co-founder Jain.As if that was not enough of a challenge, Ather decided to design, engineer and manufacture the entire product in-house, including the battery pack, motor, software platform and charging network. This marked it apart in the crowd of Indian startups that flooded the electric two-wheeler market relying on imports from China and making news for the wrong reasons, including getting into a kerfuffle with the government for their questionable claims to subsidy. Some of them are out, some on their way out.In contrast, Ather has nearly half its people working in research and development, unheard of in an Indian company of its size.A new two-wheeler order?This is hardly a David versus two Goliaths. In Ather’s corner is Hero MotoCorp, the world’s largest two-wheeler maker and its largest shareholder which in August increased its equity in the startup from 29.9 percent to 32.8 percent by infusing another ₹1,758 crore.Harshavardhan Chitale, Hero MotoCorp’s CEO, says this shows conviction in the long-term potential of electric mobility in India. “Importantly, this investment is complementary to, and does not diminish, our commitment to Vida.” Vida is Hero’s own electric two-wheeler brand.Ather has turned in profits on the basis of earnings before interest, tax, depreciation, and amortisation (Ebitda)—a widely followed metric for the financial health of a company. Clearly, the unusual bets are paying off.“We believed a strong premiumising market will allow the creation of strong product brands, brands that will build great experiences, like what Apple has done,” says Mehta.Electric was a new powertrain when Ather embraced it. There was no local supply chain and no one who had done it before to learn from. Ather had to develop the manufacturing process along with the product, says Sanjeev Kumar Singh, its chief operating officer.The manufacturing process is feeling the pangs to scale up. With the US-Iran war adding to the volatility in fuel prices, more consumers are veering towards electric. “When we were at 23,000 a month in January, we thought we will have 50 percent growth over the next 12 months. It came in three months. We have now hit a capacity constraint, and things will not change because the demand far exceeds what we can produce,” says Mehta.Also Read: Ather enters mass EV market, now targets 90% of India’s e scooter segmentIn August, Ather’s retail sales rose by 50 percent, behind the industry (67 percent), behind TVS (90 percent) and behind Bajaj (235 percent). Naturally, Ather is losing share in a growing market. TVS is the largest electric two-wheeler maker, with a 26.7 percent share of the market as of August. Bajaj is second with 22.4 percent. Ather’s share, 18.4 percent in March, has slipped to 15.7 percent.Mehta maintains there is demand for nearly 15,000 of its scooters every month that it is not able to meet. Its current annual capacity is 420,000. There is a new factory with an initial capacity of 500,000 a year which is likely to start churning out e-scooters by the end of this year. The second phase, as planned, will add another 500,000 a year.Rising stakes, higher gambitsAther was the first two-wheeler company in the world to put a touchscreen on the dashboard—no small feat in the Indian weather—and integrate Google Maps into it. The 450, which the company calls the “bike of scooters”, was the fastest accelerating made-in-India scooter at the time of its launch in 2018.Bikash Jyoti Biswas, Ather’s first employee and now its head of design, says the idea is to be differentiated. That differentiation pays off. Fourteen percent of Ather’s revenue now comes from the non-vehicle segment, largely its software, similar to premium motorcycle maker Royal Enfield’s.Ather designed its own charging connector, since adopted by the Bureau of Indian Standards as the national standard. It runs Ather Grid, a network of more than 6,100 fast chargers in 370 cities, the largest fast-charging network for two-wheelers in India.That said, the stakes have risen to their highest level ever. The scooter Mehta launched that sunny August morning is built on a new platform and is the first true mass market product that was meant to be such. It uses a steel unibody chassis and has a metal body, a construction more commonly seen in conventional scooters. Ather’s earlier products use aluminium frame architecture and plastic body panels.Changes like these allow Ather to have better margins on the Konarc, and take the fight to TVS and Bajaj. The founders, both of them 37 this year, expect the base variant to sell the most.Also Read: TVS Motor to ramp up EV capacity by up to 25 percent by year-endBattle criesOhers are not resting on their oars.TVS and Bajaj Auto are increasing their electric vehicle capacities by at least 25 percent. One of their biggest strengths is the thriving ICE (internal combustion engine) two-wheeler business, which yields cash with generosity and gives them the ammunition to fight the electric battle with strong bulwarks.HMSI has so far failed to replicate its ICE success in electric. But it is not blind to the opportunity. “Some day Honda will get serious about electric and, with its dealer network, it can take away a large chunk of the market in no time,” says Deepesh Rathore, founder of consultancy firm InsightEV.Then there are the other startups in the fray. Simple Energy, Greaves Electric Mobility, BGauss and River Mobility have all raised money this year.The biggest fundraise was by Yamaha-backed River Mobility, a Bengaluru company that raised $120 million in August and is setting up a new plant whose capacity will be seven to eight times the current factory’s 120,000.It is preparing to come after the same customers as Ather.River has a 3 percent market share with only one scooter, the Indie, which is priced at ₹1.56 lakh. That Yamaha—a company known for quality—is comfortable selling a scooter made by River under its own name as the EC-06 says something about how seriously the Japanese company takes River’s manufacturing.“We are looking at a 7 to 10 percent market share by March 2028,” says River’s co-founder and CEO Aravind Mani. article_sentences: New Delhi: An umpire selected by the captain of a cricket team that eventually wins would always be suspected over his decisions even if they are correct, Supreme Court judge Dipankar Datta said on Wednesday to highlight that the Executive will have an “effective” veto in the selection of the Chief Election Commissioner and election commissioners.

Using this cricket metaphor, Justice Datta was extremely critical of the fact that a three-member panel, comprising the Prime Minister, the Leader of Opposition and a Union minister, selects the CEC and election commissioners.
If free and fair elections are to be ensured, it is axiomatic that the Election Commission (EC) must not only be an independent body but also be seen to act independently, he said.

Justice Datta headed a bench, also comprising Justice Satish Chandra Sharma, which gave split opinions on whether a batch of pleas challenging the validity of a 2023 law that excludes the CJI from the panel for selecting the chief election commissioner (CEC) and election commissioners should be referred to a larger constitution bench.

Dealing with the issue of independence and neutrality, Justice Datta noted the submissions of petitioners that the inclusion of a minister in the panel denuded the selection committee of institutional neutrality.
“If the said Selection Committee were to function, the decision would invariably be 2:1, on paper, in favour of the executive and, in practice, of whoever is the ruling party.
With two members from the executive being part of the Selection Committee, the executive has an effective veto,” he said.

Referring to discussion during the hearing, he said it was quite unlikely that the minister would take a stand against the Prime Minister in case of a difference of opinion between the Prime Minister and the Leader of Opposition.
“The presence of likelihood of a ‘no’ is striking enough to colour the perception of the Selection Committee; the probabilities and certainties of the ‘no’ matter little.
Thus, the challengers of the law contend, even if the appointments are meritorious, the process does not pass the perception test.

“The bottom line of the argument runs thus: it would not be a fallacious metaphor if it is said that since the umpire is picked by the captain of one side in a cricket match and his team wins, even if the decisions taken by such umpire are correct, it has the patina of suspicion, for, at the end of the day, the umpire has effectively been chosen by the winning captain,” he said.
Justice Sharma differed with the views of Justice Datta and batted for referring the pleas to a larger bench while terming the issue as important.

However, NSE’s stock markets debut lacked investor euphoria. On Thursday, it was listed at Rs1,800 on the BSE, merely 1 percent premium over its issue price of Rs1,785 per share.While the Rs22,568.94 crore issue ranks NSE as India's second largest initial public offering (IPO), its larger significance lies in the culmination of one of the country's longest-running and closely watched listing sagas. The exchange's IPO plans were stalled for years amid regulatory concerns and governance issues. The listing also provides investors a direct stake in the country's dominant equity and derivatives trading platform.NSE's path to the public markets has been rather rough. It had first filed for an IPO for nearly Rs10,000-crore offer-for-sale (OFS) in 2016. However, its listing ambitions were put on hold after markets regulator, the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi), had asked NSE to withdraw the application amid compliance and governance concerns stemming from the co-location scandal. It suffered another setback in April 2019 when Sebi barred NSE from the securities markets for six months in connection with the co-location controversy.Also Read: The NSE paradox: Why market dominance may be a liabilityThe co-location controversy refers to allegations that certain brokers received preferential access to the exchange's trading systems through its co-location facility, giving them a speed advantage in executing trades. After years of regulatory scrutiny, litigations and appeals, NSE subsequently sought to resolve the matter through Sebi's settlement mechanism, agreeing to pay Rs1,491 crore to settle the co-location and related dark-fibre cases, removing a key regulatory overhang ahead of its IPO.Investors’ appetite for NSEThe issue with a price band of Rs1,700-1,785 per share was overall subscribed nearly six times with institutional investors bidding at 12.68 times and retail investors 1.4 times. The three-day sale which ended on September 21 was a pure OFS. It had already raised Rs6,746.2 crore from anchor investors, including Life Insurance Corporation of India (LIC), Norway’s Government Pension Fund Global, Abu Dhabi Investment Authority (ADIA), GIC Singapore, Fidelity and Societe Generale, among others.According to analysts at Bajaj Financial Securities, NSE’s continued expansion across asset classes and financial products may support further business development, while trading volumes and transaction activity remain key variables. “At the upper price band, NSE is valued at 42.9 times price-to-earnings (PE),” they say.The sheer size of the NSE IPO did little to deter investors. The NSE IPO attracted bids worth more than Rs90,000 crore, the highest ever for a public issue in India. Despite its size, the offering drew strong investor interest, making it the most subscribed among India's five largest IPOs. In comparison, Hyundai Motor India's Rs27,859-crore IPO, the country's largest public issue, was subscribed 2.3 times when it had hit the market in 2024.For perspective, LIC's Rs20,557.23-crore IPO was subscribed nearly 3 times, Paytm parent One 97 Communications' Rs18,300-crore offering received bids for 1.9 times the shares on offer and Tata Capital's Rs15,511.87-crore IPO was subscribed 1.95 times.Also Read: Ashishkumar Chauhan: The man who built NSE, and came back to rebuild trustMarket monopolyNSE is a market leader with a monopoly in cash equities, equity futures, equity options, exchange traded currency futures and exchange-traded currency options. NSE has been the largest stock exchange in India in terms of total turnover in cash market and total turnover in equity derivatives from FY2001 (from June 2000) to FY26, according to a report by Redseer Strategy Consultants. Globally, for seven consecutive years, it is at the top spot in equity derivatives contracts traded.Cash market average daily turnover (ADTO) saw strong growth between FY14 and FY26, rising from Rs13,300 crore to Rs1.1 lakh crore, reflecting deeper market penetration and increased investor participation. Retail investors have surged with increase in mobile-based trading, while co-location along with an increase in algo-trading is a noticeable trend in this segment, highlighting participation of institutional investors and traders.As of FY26, NSE commands 92.99 percent market share in cash equities based on total turnover, 99.79 percent in equity futures (based on total turnover), 74.71 percent in equity options (based on premium turnover), 99.48 percent in exchange traded currency futures (based on total turnover) and 100 percent for exchange-traded currency options (based on total industry premium turnover) in India.In FY26, NSE recorded the highest operating Ebitda margin (66.85 percent) and one of the highest net profit margins (50.98 percent of total income) among global listed exchanges. NSE's revenue from operations grew at a 5.98 percent CAGR to Rs16,601.3 crore in FY26 from Rs14,780 crore in FY24, while profit for the year grew at 11.37 percent CAGR to Rs10,302 crore from Rs8,305.74 crore over the same period.Also Read: Ashishkumar Chauhan on how NSE became a model of resilienceThe concentration riskNSE relies heavily on derivatives revenues at a time when regulators are re-examining the social and financial costs of speculative trading. The market regulator’s move to curb excessive speculation in derivatives, NSE's greatest revenue engine, could increasingly become risky.The derivative segment has seen multiple regulatory changes from the second half of FY25, especially in the derivatives market, as regulators are focussed on protecting retail investors. Average daily trading volume (ADTV) in equity futures declined to Rs159,443.21 crore in FY26 from Rs185,901.44 crore in FY25, and equity options ADTV (premium) to Rs57,661.75 crore from Rs62,448.66 crore in the same time period.NSE’s revenues are intrinsically tied to volume and value of transactions, number of new listings and breadth of investor participation. In FY26, trading services accounted for 78.65 percent of revenue from operations. From FY23 to FY25, NSE’s total revenue grew at a CAGR of 23 percent, positioning it among the top three listed exchanges globally in terms of two-year total revenue growth, according to the Redseer report.“Transaction charges formed 78.6 percent of FY26 operating revenue, including 60.2 percent from options, exposing earnings to regulatory changes, competition, pricing pressure and weaker market activity,” says Vishal Narnolia, analyst, ICICI Securities.Dependence on transaction charges for revenue indicates higher sensitivity to market volumes and trading cycles. In contrast, global peers like Intercontinental Exchange, NASDAQ, London Stock Exchange, Japan Exchange Group and Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing have diversified revenue streams, which result in a more stable earning profile compared to volume-driven Indian exchanges.NSE continues to face legacy regulatory and legal matters whose outcomes create reputational, operational and financial overhang. Adverse outcomes or additional regulatory proceedings could result in financial liabilities, operational restrictions and reputational consequences,” says Narnolia.

The Supreme Court today (24 September) has laid down a set of safeguards to prevent the misuse of the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012 (POCSO Act) as a weapon in matrimonial and child custody disputes.

The safeguards were laid down while quashing an FIR alleging sexual assault of a minor girl by her father, after a probe by the Central Investigation Agency (CBI) found the allegations to be unreliable.

A bench of Justice JB Pardiwala and Justice KV Viswanathan was dealing with a batch of appeals arising out of a bitter and long-drawn custody battle between a divorced couple, referred to in the judgment as 'R' (father) and 'E' (mother), over their minor daughter 'M'.
The Court has flagged the growing misuse of POCSO Act in matrimonial disputes.

Referring to precedents like Geddam Jhansi v State of Telangana, Achin Gupta v State of Haryana, Ishwar Chand Sharma v State of UP, and Kerala High Court's Suhara v Muhammed Jaleel, the bench noted a worrying trend of spouses filing false POCSO complaints to gain leverage in custody battles or extract better settlements.

The bench observed that while Section 22 of the POCSO Act penalises false complaints, “by the time Section 22 is invoked substantial damage would be caused to the party falsely charged,” in the form of either prolonged incarceration or adverse impact on pending guardianship or custody proceedings.
It therefore held that “certain precautions must be taken, within the four corners of the law, to prevent such harm from befalling the accused.”

“Any precaution we envision to prevent irreparable harm to the accused in certain contexts and circumstances must, therefore, not run counter to the stated object of the Act, or dilute the stringency with which such offences are meant to be treated.

What is needed is a balancing exercise: precautions that neither dilute the object of the Act nor weaken its provisions, while allowing sufficient leeway to ensure that irreparable harm is not caused to the accused,” the bench further clarified.
The bench further clarified that the safeguards would apply only where two threshold conditions are met.
One, an offence under the POCSO Act is alleged to have been committed by a parent or family member living under the same roof as the child victim.

stories.headline: Karnataka HC upholds land acquisition to protect DRDO’s Centre for Artificial Intelligence and Robotics project area
stories.title: Karnataka HC upholds land acquisition to protect DRDO’s Centre for Artificial Intelligence and Robotics project area
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: A Division Bench of the Karnataka High Court has upheld the acquisition of about 1.27 acres of additional land in Bennegahalli in Bengaluru for the Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO), bringing to an end a decades-old legal dispute.

The acquisition was set aside by a single judge in 2014 on the ground that landowners were not properly heard during the process of considering objections, but the Division Bench has now validated the acquisition, which was vital for the DRDO to protect the area around its sensitive Centre for Artificial Intelligence and Robotics (CAIR).

A Division Bench comprising Justice D.K. Singh and Justice H. Shanthi Bhushan passed the order while allowing the appeals filed way back in 2015 by the Union government and the DRDO challenging the single judge’s order.
The Bench noted the long and chequered history of the acquisition, which began with a preliminary notification in 1987.
After prolonged litigation and a compromise before the Supreme Court, a fresh notification was issued in 2005 after the earlier award lapsed.

The single judge, the Bench said, could have asked the land acquisition officer to hear afresh the objections of the landowners instead of quashing the acquisition process itself, as the land was acquired not for any ordinary purpose but for protecting the defence project area adjacent to these lands.
The Bench emphasised that the lands in question were surrounded by areas already handed over to the DRDO and fell within the protected area of the CAIR facility.

The requirement of a compact and protected area is a relevant consideration in a defence acquisition, the Bench said, while pointing out that quashing of acquisition for some deficiency in consideration of objections does not appear to be commensurate with the nature of the alleged procedural lapse when the land is acquired for a project of national importance.
“We are conscious that the rights of private landowners cannot be disregarded merely because the acquisition is for a public purpose.

At the same time, the rights of the landowners have to be harmonised with the larger constitutional obligation of the State to protect the nation and to provide the infrastructure necessary for national defence and security,” the Bench observed.
Meanwhile, the Bench made it clear that the rights of the landowners, in respect of compensation, award, apportionment, or disbursement, remain protected under the applicable law.

At the same time, the rights of the landowners have to be harmonised with the larger constitutional obligation of the State to protect the nation and to provide the infrastructure necessary for national defence and security,” the Bench observed.

The Bench noted the long and chequered history of the acquisition, which began with a preliminary notification in 1987.

The acquisition was set aside by a single judge in 2014 on the ground that landowners were not properly heard during the process of considering objections, but the Division Bench has now validated the acquisition, which was vital for the DRDO to protect the area around its sensitive Centre for Artificial Intelligence and Robotics (CAIR).

A Division Bench comprising Justice D.K. Singh and Justice H. Shanthi Bhushan passed the order while allowing the appeals filed way back in 2015 by the Union government and the DRDO challenging the single judge’s order.

stories.headline: India’s market regulator SEBI widens FPI access to commodity derivatives
stories.title: India’s market regulator SEBI widens FPI access to commodity derivatives
stories.summary: At its latest Board meeting, SEBI widened foreign portfolio investor access to exchange-traded commodity derivatives, confirming a CNBC-TV18 report earlier this month that the regulator was set to open up more non-agricultural contracts to FPIs.
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence

article_sentences: The Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) Board, at its meeting on Thursday, approved wider participation by foreign portfolio investors (FPIs) in exchange-traded commodity derivatives, allowing them to access a broader set of non-agricultural contracts.
The SEBI Board’s decision confirms a CNBC-TV18 news break from September 4, which reported that the regulator was set to allow FPIs to participate in commodity derivatives.
Sources had told CNBC-TV18 that SEBI was expected to permit FPI trading in non-cash-settled, non-agricultural commodity derivatives, broadly along the lines proposed in its consultation paper.

The market regulator has approved FPI participation in non-agricultural index derivatives, irrespective of whether the underlying contracts are cash-settled, as well as non-cash-settled non-agricultural commodity derivatives.
However, FPIs participating in non-cash-settled non-agricultural commodity derivatives will have to exit their positions before any delivery obligation arises.
Under the new framework, FPIs will have to square off their positions before the start of the Tender Period, which begins three days before the expiry of a contract.
They will also not be allowed to increase their positions from the T-3 day.
If an FPI fails to exit its position, the open position can be transferred to its trading member or trading-cum-clearing member (TM/TCM), subject to the agreed arrangements.

Before an FPI is enabled to trade on an exchange, it will have to enter into an agreement with its TM/TCM specifying how its positions will be handled, including arrangements for squaring off positions ahead of the delivery obligation.
SEBI said the transfer of an FPI’s open position to the TM/TCM will be treated as a trade and will attract applicable statutory levies.
The regulator said the move is aimed at deepening liquidity in the commodity derivatives market, while ensuring that FPIs do not enter the physical delivery process.

The move is expected to benefit commodity exchanges and trading platforms, including Multi Commodity Exchange of India (MCX), BSE and NSE, by potentially broadening participation and liquidity in eligible contracts.
